deep.reconstruction: There is no mathematics on this page. It is a library request or loan slip, not a working sheet. In ink, at the top, it reads: 'Euleri Institutiones Calculi Integralis. 2 Voll. Ed. 2a. Petropoli 1792'. This asks for two volumes of the second (St Petersburg) edition of Euler's Institutiones Calculi Integralis. That edition appeared in 1792-1794 in four volumes; the first edition was 1768-1770 in three volumes. At the lower right is the borrower's signature in ink, 'B Riemann', with a short word below it that I read as 'Orgel' or 'Ogsl.'; I cannot read it securely. It is probably a status or address abbreviation. The large pencil writing looks like a librarian's hand. It gives a shelf mark or register number, roughly 'S/12/341' (or '8/12/341'), a word like 'Matter' or 'Matth.', and a large scrawled initial or paraph with a stroke. In red at the lower left is a note that looks like a date, probably 'Dec. 11. 51' (11 December 1851), possibly 'Nov.'. This would be the loan or return date in the Göttingen university library. At the upper right is a later archival folio number in pencil, '213'. Historically, the slip documents that Riemann borrowed Euler's integral calculus, probably around December 1851. That is the period of his doctoral dissertation on complex function theory, defended in November 1851, and of his work towards the Habilitation. Euler's treatise covers elliptic-type integrals, differential equations and the hypergeometric series. These are topics Riemann later took up, for example in his 1857 work on the hypergeometric function P-function. The next page holds unrelated algebraic scratch work in s, a and b, written on the back of or beside the slip.

That Riemann read Euler's integral calculus is unsurprising; Göttingen loan records of Riemann are known to historians, for example from Neuenschwander's studies of his library borrowing. It is only a minor biographical datum.
transcription_corrections: '1/12/341' is more likely a library shelf or register mark such as 'S/12/341' or '8/12/341' in pencil, written by the librarian rather than by Riemann.
'Matter' is an uncertain pencil word, possibly an abbreviation such as 'Math.' or a librarian's name or mark; it is followed by a large pencil paraph, not text.
'Rgsl' under the signature reads more like 'Orgsl.' or 'Orgel'; it remains uncertain, probably an abbreviation of the borrower's status or address.
'Dev. 11. 5l.' in red is most plausibly a date, 'Dec. 11. 51' (11 December 1851), possibly 'Nov. 11. 51'.
'Ed 2a' is written with a monogram-like 'Ed' followed by '2a' with an underlined superscript a (editio secunda).
A pencil folio number '213' at the upper right is omitted from the transcription.
